claim: Microglia are the resident immune cells of the brain.
source: Microglia, the resident immune cells of the brain, play a complex role in health and disease.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract defining microglia.

claim: Microglia actively survey the brain parenchyma by physically interacting with other cells.
source: They actively survey the brain parenchyma by physically interacting with other cells and structurally shaping the brain.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known function of microglia.

claim: CA3 to CA1 input is sufficient to modulate microglial process motility.
source: We found that CA3 to CA1 input is sufficient to modulate microglial process motility.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: More dendritic spines emerged in mice after awake compared to anesthetized imaging.
source: Simultaneously, more dendritic spines emerged in mice after awake compared to anesthetized imaging.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: The rate of microglial contacts with individual dendritic spines and dendrites was associated with the stability, removal, and emergence of dendritic spines.
source: Interestingly, the rate of microglial contacts with individual dendritic spines and dendrites was associated with the stability, removal, and emergence of dendritic spines.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: Microglia might sense neuronal activity via neurotransmitter release and actively participate in synaptic rewiring of the hippocampal neural network during adulthood.
source: These results suggest that microglia might sense neuronal activity via neurotransmitter release and actively participate in synaptic rewiring of the hippocampal neural network during adulthood.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results stated in the abstract, based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: Under physiological conditions, microglia are sessile, highly ramified, and plastic cells that constantly scan their environment with fine processes.
source: Under physiological conditions, microglia are sessile, highly ramified, and plastic cells that constantly scan their environment with fine processes, an activity referred to as microglial motility (Davalos et al., 2005; Nimmerjahn et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Microglial motility is ATP-dependent.
source: This remarkable degree of cellular plasticity enables microglia to detect and quickly react to even the subtlest changes of tissue homeostasis within their microenvironment – a process shown to be ATP-dependent (Davalos et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Davalos et al., 2005.

claim: Microglia have been linked to a number of neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease.
source: While microglia have been linked to a number of neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease (Heneka et al., 2014; Ransohoff, 2016), little is known about their physiological function under healthy conditions (Tay et al., 2017; Tremblay et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Little is known about the physiological function of microglia under healthy conditions.
source: While microglia have been linked to a number of neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease (Heneka et al., 2014; Ransohoff, 2016), little is known about their physiological function under healthy conditions (Tay et al., 2017; Tremblay et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Interfering with neuronal activity in vivo using tetrodotoxin (TTX) and bicuculline led to inconsistent findings regarding microglial process motility.
source: During the discovery of microglial motility, the hypothesis was tested as to whether process motility related to neuronal activity, yet interfering with neuronal activity in vivo using tetrodotoxin (TTX) and bicuculline led to inconsistent findings (Nimmerjahn et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Nimmerjahn et al., 2005.

claim: There is no current consensus on the impact of anesthesia on microglial motility in vivo.
source: These results may have been confounded by the use of anesthetics like isoflurane, although there is no current consensus on the impact of anesthesia on microglial motility in vivo.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field based on the literature review.

claim: Under fentanyl/midazolam/dexmedetomidine anesthesia in vivo, cortical microglia increased their process area and surveillance territory.
source: Under fentanyl/midazolam/dexmedetomidine (Stowell et al., 2019) or isoflurane (Liu et al., 2019) anesthesia in vivo, cortical microglia increased their process area and surveillance territory.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Stowell et al., 2019 and Liu et al., 2019.

claim: Under isoflurane anesthesia in vivo, cortical microglia increased their process area and surveillance territory.
source: Under fentanyl/midazolam/dexmedetomidine (Stowell et al., 2019) or isoflurane (Liu et al., 2019) anesthesia in vivo, cortical microglia increased their process area and surveillance territory.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Stowell et al., 2019 and Liu et al., 2019.

claim: Isoflurane anesthesia decreased microglia motility in acute slice preparations.
source: However, contradictory effects have been described while using isolflurane anesthesia, showing decreased microglia motility in response to isoflurane in acute slice preparations (Madry et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Madry et al., 2018.

claim: Microglia motility is positively correlated to neuronal activity in vivo in the cortex.
source: Further, a recent study also described microglia motility being positively correlated to neuronal activity in vivo in the cortex (Hristovska et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hristovska et al., 2022.

claim: Diverging findings on microglial motility might in part be due to different means of preparation, specimen age, and/or brain region specificity.
source: These diverging findings might in part be due to different means of preparation, specimen age, and/or brain region specificity, as microglia display a high degree of region-dependent diversity (Grabert et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the literature and supported by a citation to Grabert et al., 2016.

claim: Microglia display a high degree of region-dependent diversity.
source: These diverging findings might in part be due to different means of preparation, specimen age, and/or brain region specificity, as microglia display a high degree of region-dependent diversity (Grabert et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Grabert et al., 2016.

claim: Evidence from Ca2+ imaging in zebrafish suggests a reciprocal relationship between microglial motility and neuronal activity, with decreased Ca2-transient frequencies upon microglial contact with neurons.
source: Evidence from Ca2+ imaging in zebrafish suggests a reciprocal relationship between microglial motility and neuronal activity, with decreased Ca2-transient frequencies upon microglial contact with neurons (Li et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2012.

claim: Lowering neuronal activity by inducing hypothermia and applying TTX reduced the frequency of microglial contacts with dendritic spines in the visual and somatosensory cortex.
source: Lowering neuronal activity by inducing hypothermia and applying TTX reduced the frequency of microglial contacts with dendritic spines in the visual and somatosensory cortex, although microglial motility was not directly measured in this particular study (Wake et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Wake et al., 2009.

claim: In the visual cortex, microglial motility was reduced in mice kept in darkness.
source: Moreover, in the visual cortex microglial motility was reduced in mice kept in darkness, whereas it increased in mice re-exposed to light after a dark period (Tremblay et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tremblay et al., 2010.

claim: In the visual cortex, microglial motility increased in mice re-exposed to light after a dark period.
source: Moreover, in the visual cortex microglial motility was reduced in mice kept in darkness, whereas it increased in mice re-exposed to light after a dark period (Tremblay et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tremblay et al., 2010.

claim: Microglial contact rate increased before dendritic spines were eliminated during a critical period of developmental plasticity in the visual cortex.
source: The same study found that microglial contact rate increased before dendritic spines were eliminated during a critical period of developmental plasticity, suggesting a role for microglia in shaping post-synapses.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tremblay et al., 2010 (implied from 'The same study').

claim: During early development in the mouse cortex, microglial contacts at dendrites induced the formation of new dendritic filopodial spines in awake, but not anesthetized mice.
source: During early development in the mouse cortex, microglial contacts at dendrites also induced the formation of new dendritic filopodial spines in awake, but not anesthetized mice (Miyamoto et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Miyamoto et al., 2016.

claim: Removal of microglia from the brain of adult mice reduced motor learning-induced/BDNF-dependent formation of new dendritic spines in the motor cortex.
source: Additionally, removal of microglia from the brain of adult mice reduced motor learning-induced/BDNF-dependent formation of new dendritic spines in the motor cortex (Parkhurst et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Parkhurst et al., 2013.

claim: Recent data from in vitro studies showed a relationship of long-term potentiation and spine contact rates with microglia in the hippocampus.
source: Yet, recent data from in vitro studies showed a relationship of long-term potentiation and spine contact rates with microglia in the hippocampus (Pfeiffer et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Pfeiffer et al., 2016.

claim: Pre-synapses – but not post-synapses – were eliminated by trogocytosis by microglia during development in hippocampal slice cultures.
source: Further, pre-synapses – but not post-synapses – were eliminated by trogocytosis (non-apoptotic uptake of membrane components by immune cells), while filopodial spine formation was induced by microglia during development in hippocampal slice cultures (Weinhard et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Weinhard et al., 2018.

claim: Filopodial spine formation was induced by microglia during development in hippocampal slice cultures.
source: Further, pre-synapses – but not post-synapses – were eliminated by trogocytosis (non-apoptotic uptake of membrane components by immune cells), while filopodial spine formation was induced by microglia during development in hippocampal slice cultures (Weinhard et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Weinhard et al., 2018.

claim: Microglial responses to neuronal stimulation in the hippocampus were only detectable during early post-natal stages and absent during adulthood in vitro.
source: Additional in vitro experiments indicated that microglial responses to neuronal stimulation in the hippocampus were only detectable during early post-natal stages and absent during adulthood (Logiacco et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Logiacco et al., 2021.

claim: Microglia are by far the most plastic cells in the CNS.
source: The interplay between microglia and synapses is of particular interest, as microglia are by far the most plastic cells in the CNS.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about microglia.

claim: Microglia have been shown to be critical for synaptogenesis and synaptic integrity during developmental stages.
source: Whereas microglia have been shown to be critical for synaptogenesis and synaptic integrity during developmental stages (Miyamoto et al., 2016; Schafer et al., 2012; Stevens et al., 2007; Tremblay et al., 2010), little is known about their contribution to structural plasticity in the hippocampus during adulthood.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Little is known about microglia's contribution to structural plasticity in the hippocampus during adulthood.
source: Whereas microglia have been shown to be critical for synaptogenesis and synaptic integrity during developmental stages (Miyamoto et al., 2016; Schafer et al., 2012; Stevens et al., 2007; Tremblay et al., 2010), little is known about their contribution to structural plasticity in the hippocampus during adulthood.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The role of microglia in CNS homeostasis might differ between CNS development and adulthood.
source: Thus, it is critical to understand the nature and functional properties of microglia-synapse interactions, especially during adulthood, as the role of microglia in CNS homeostasis might differ between CNS development and adulthood (Mosser et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Mosser et al., 2017.

claim: Microglial fine process motility has not been examined in vivo in the hippocampus up until now.
source: Microglial fine process motility has not been examined in vivo in the hippocampus up until now, and recent findings implicate a more heterogeneous role of microglia throughout different brain regions than previously assumed (Grabert et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the current study.

claim: Mice used in the study were heterozygous for both Thy1-YFP and Cx3cr1-GFP alleles.
source: Mice were heterozygous for both alleles (Thy1-YFPtg/wt::Cx3cr1-GFPki/wt) and between 7 and 10 months of age.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental animals used.

claim: Mice used in the study were between 7 and 10 months of age.
source: Mice were heterozygous for both alleles (Thy1-YFPtg/wt::Cx3cr1-GFPki/wt) and between 7 and 10 months of age.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental animals used.

claim: CX3CR1-GFP mice are haploinsufficient for the fractalkine receptor (CX3CR1).
source: Of note, Cx3cr1-GFPki/wt microglia are haploinsufficient for the fractalkine receptor (CX3CR1).
evidence: This is a statement about the genetic characteristics of the mouse model used.

claim: In an elaborated transcriptome analysis of mice with complete loss or haploinsufficiency of CX3CR1 compared to the wildtype (WT) condition, major differences were found at a younger age (2 months), whereas WT and heterozygous mice cluster closer together in older mice 1–2 years of age.
source: However, in an elaborated transcriptome analysis of mice with complete loss or haploinsufficiency of CX3CR1 compared to the wildtype (WT) condition, major differences were found at a younger age (2 months), whereas WT and heterozygous mice cluster closer together in older mice 1–2 years of age (Gyoneva et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Gyoneva et al., 2019.

claim: Under isoflurane anesthesia (1.0% isoflurane in oxygen), microglia showed reduced fine process motility compared to the awake condition.
source: Under isoflurane anesthesia (1.0% isoflurane in oxygen), microglia showed reduced fine process motility compared to the awake condition (60.2% ± 2.7% anesthesia vs. 69.9% ± 2.8% awake; Figure 1d; Figure 1—videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, supported by data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Isoflurane acts primarily by prolonging GABAergic transmission, thus inhibiting neuronal activity.
source: Isoflurane acts primarily by prolonging GABAergic transmission, thus inhibiting neuronal activity (Goltstein et al., 2015; Noda and Takahashi, 2015; Vahle-Hinz et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: 1% isoflurane anesthesia significantly reduced Ca2+ event rate as a marker of neuronal activity by more than 50% in hippocampal CA1 neurons.
source: We confirmed that 1% isoflurane anesthesia significantly reduced Ca2+ event rate as a marker of neuronal activity by more than 50% in hippocampal CA1 neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 1—videos 3 and 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Topical application of TTX (50 µM) significantly decreased microglial motility in awake mice, even below the levels of these same mice under anesthesia.
source: This pharmacological manipulation significantly decreased microglial motility in awake mice, even below the levels of these same mice under anesthesia (Figure 1d; 69.9% ± 2.8% awake vs. 52,8±1.2% awake plus TTX).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, supported by data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: CNO-mediated silencing of CA3 and CA1 neurons significantly reduced microglial motility.
source: CNO-mediated silencing of CA3 and CA1 neurons significantly reduced microglial motility (Figure 2—figure supplement 1g; 71.2%±1.5% vehicle vs. 58.7%±1.8% CNO).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1g.

claim: In respective CA3 regions, 74% of neurons expressed hM4D(Gi).
source: In respective CA3 regions, 74% of neurons expressed hM4D(Gi) (Figure 2b–d) or 68% of neurons expressed hM3D(Gq) (Figure 2f–h).
evidence: This is a quantification of DREADD expression, supported by data shown in Figure 2b-d.

claim: In respective CA3 regions, 68% of neurons expressed hM3D(Gq).
source: In respective CA3 regions, 74% of neurons expressed hM4D(Gi) (Figure 2b–d) or 68% of neurons expressed hM3D(Gq) (Figure 2f–h).
evidence: This is a quantification of DREADD expression, supported by data shown in Figure 2f-h.

claim: CNO-mediated activation of hM3D(Gq)-expressing CA3 neurons significantly increased axonal Ca2+ event frequency compared to vehicle injections.
source: CNO-mediated activation of hM3D(Gq)-expressing CA3 neurons significantly increased axonal Ca2+ event frequency compared to vehicle injections, suggesting effective DREADD expression and agonist delivery (Figure 2—figure supplement 2g; Figure 2—videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a validation finding from the study, supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2g.

claim: Inhibition of CA3 input to CA1 neurons via the Schaffer collaterals significantly decreased microglial motility in the SR.
source: Inhibition of CA3 input to CA1 neurons via the Schaffer collaterals significantly decreased microglial motility in the SR (Figure 2j and k; 66.1%±3% vehicle vs. 54.3 ± 3% CNO).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, supported by data shown in Figure 2j and k.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of hM3D(Gq) transfected CA3 neurons significantly increased microglial motility.
source: Conversely chemogenetic activation of hM3D(Gq) transfected CA3 neurons significantly increased microglial motility (Figure 2j and l; 56.6% ± 1.8% vehicle vs. 66.6%±2.2% CNO).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, supported by data shown in Figure 2j and l.

claim: Manipulation of CA3 input to CA1 is sufficient to alter microglial motility in the SR of CA1.
source: These data indicate that manipulation of CA3 input to CA1 is sufficient to alter microglial motility in the SR of CA1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claim: CA3 input to CA1 via Schaffer collaterals is an important pathway of the hippocampus involved in spatial information processing and learning.
source: CA3 input to CA1 via Schaffer collaterals is an important pathway of the hippocampus involved in spatial information processing and learning.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about hippocampal circuitry.

claim: CA3 axons form synapses with dendritic spines of CA1 neurons in the SR and their stimulation can lead to long-term synaptic plasticity.
source: CA3 axons form synapses with dendritic spines of CA1 neurons in the SR and their stimulation can lead to long-term synaptic plasticity (Luscher and Malenka, 2012; Takeuchi et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Microglia have been shown to increase their process length and prolong their contacts with dendritic spines in hippocampal slices during long-term potentiation in situ.
source: Microglia have been shown to increase their process length and prolong their contacts with dendritic spines in hippocampal slices during long-term potentiation in situ (Pfeiffer et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Pfeiffer et al., 2016.

claim: A significant increase in spine density was observed 2 days after awake imaging compared to anesthetized imaging.
source: Here, we observed a significant increase in spine density and significantly higher fractions of gained vs. lost spines 2 days after awake imaging (Figure 3c–f).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, supported by data shown in Figure 3c-f.

claim: Significantly higher fractions of gained vs. lost spines were observed 2 days after awake imaging.
source: Here, we observed a significant increase in spine density and significantly higher fractions of gained vs. lost spines 2 days after awake imaging (Figure 3c–f).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, supported by data shown in Figure 3c-f.

claim: A substantial fraction of dendritic spine turnover was spatially clustered along the dendrites of CA1 pyramidal neurons (i.e. within 4 µm along the same dendrite; 55% of observed turnover).
source: Moreover, a substantial fraction of dendritic spine turnover was spatially clustered along the dendrites of CA1 pyramidal neurons (i.e. within 4 µm along the same dendrite; 55% of observed turnover, see Figure 3—figure supplement 1a-c).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a-c.

claim: Similar findings of clustered spine turnover have previously been reported for dendrites of excitatory neurons in the hippocampus, somatosensory, motor, visual, and retrosplenial cortices.
source: Similar findings have previously been reported for dendrites of excitatory neurons in the hippocampus, somatosensory, motor, visual, and retrosplenial cortices (Bloss et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2012; Frank et al., 2018; Fu et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Microglia had significantly higher contact rate with dendritic spines under awake conditions relative to anesthetized conditions.
source: Relative to anesthetized conditions, microglia had significantly higher contact rate with dendritic spines under awake conditions (Figure 4i; 5.31±0.16 hr–1 in anesthesia vs. 7.33±0.21 hr–1 awake).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, supported by data shown in Figure 4i.

claim: There was no significant difference in contact with the dendritic shaft by microglia between awake and anesthetized conditions.
source: However, there was no significant difference in contact with the dendritic shaft by microglia between awake and anesthetized conditions (Figure 4j; 5.55±0.16 hr–1 in anesthesia vs. 6.22±0.36 hr–1 awake).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by data shown in Figure 4j.

claim: The contact frequency of gained spines was significantly increased compared to stable spines.
source: Interestingly, the contact frequency of both gained (Figure 4k; stable 5.14±0.16 hr–1 vs. gained 9.93±0.15 hr–1) and lost (Figure 4k; stable spines: 5.31±0.16 hr–1 vs. lost spines 8.37±1.12 hr–1) spines was significantly increased compared to stable spines, indicating that microglial contact frequency is positively associated with structural plasticity of dendritic spines.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, supported by data shown in Figure 4k.

claim: The contact frequency of lost spines was significantly increased compared to stable spines.
source: Interestingly, the contact frequency of both gained (Figure 4k; stable 5.14±0.16 hr–1 vs. gained 9.93±0.15 hr–1) and lost (Figure 4k; stable spines: 5.31±0.16 hr–1 vs. lost spines 8.37±1.12 hr–1) spines was significantly increased compared to stable spines, indicating that microglial contact frequency is positively associated with structural plasticity of dendritic spines.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, supported by data shown in Figure 4k.

claim: Microglial contact frequency is positively associated with structural plasticity of dendritic spines.
source: Interestingly, the contact frequency of both gained (Figure 4k; stable 5.14±0.16 hr–1 vs. gained 9.93±0.15 hr–1) and lost (Figure 4k; stable spines: 5.31±0.16 hr–1 vs. lost spines 8.37±1.12 hr–1) spines was significantly increased compared to stable spines, indicating that microglial contact frequency is positively associated with structural plasticity of dendritic spines.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 4k.

claim: Microglial contacts were more frequent at sites on the dendritic shaft where spines were gained, compared to dendritic segments where no new spines were detectable.
source: Moreover, microglial contacts were more frequent at sites on the dendritic shaft where spines were gained, compared to dendritic segments where no new spines were detectable (Figure 4k; dendritic shafts without spine gain 5.55±0.16 hr–1 vs. dendritic shafts with spine gain 9.93±0.15 hr–1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, supported by data shown in Figure 4k.

claim: Microglial contacts of dendritic spines were significantly higher where spine turnover occurred in clusters.
source: Finally, microglial contacts of dendritic spines were significantly higher where spine turnover occurred in clusters (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d), suggesting microglia might facilitate spatial reorganization of dendritic spines in the hippocampus.
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Microglia might facilitate spatial reorganization of dendritic spines in the hippocampus.
source: Finally, microglial contacts of dendritic spines were significantly higher where spine turnover occurred in clusters (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d), suggesting microglia might facilitate spatial reorganization of dendritic spines in the hippocampus.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data, based on the finding of increased microglial contacts at clustered spine turnover sites.

claim: Microglial contact frequency of spines was increased in mice under awake relative to anesthetized conditions, corresponding to increased microglial motility in response to CA3 input/neuronal activity.
source: In summary, these data show that microglial contact frequency of spines was increased in mice under awake relative to anesthetized conditions, corresponding to increased microglial motility in response to CA3 input/neuronal activity.
evidence: This is a summary statement integrating multiple findings from the study.

claim: The turnover (gain and loss) of dendritic spines correlated with higher microglial contact frequency on hippocampal CA1 neurons of adult mice.
source: Furthermore, the turnover (gain and loss) of dendritic spines correlated with higher microglial contact frequency on hippocampal CA1 neurons of adult mice.
evidence: This is a summary statement of a primary finding from the study.

claim: Elevated motility of microglia fine processes was detected in awake mice compared to the same mice under anesthetized conditions.
source: We detected elevated motility of microglia fine processes in awake mice compared to the same mice under anesthetized conditions.
evidence: This is a summary of a primary finding from the study.

claim: A modulation of microglial motility via CA3 to CA1 input was demonstrated using both pharmacological and chemogenetic approaches.
source: We further demonstrated a modulation of microglial motility via CA3 to CA1 input using both pharmacological and chemogenetic approaches.
evidence: This is a summary of a primary finding from the study.

claim: Lost spines were contacted more frequently by microglia in a preceding imaging session than stable spines.
source: Here, lost spines and dendritic stretches with a newly appearing spine were contacted more frequently by microglia in a preceding imaging session than stable spines.
evidence: This is a summary of a primary finding from the study.

claim: Dendritic stretches with a newly appearing spine were contacted more frequently by microglia in a preceding imaging session than stable spines.
source: Here, lost spines and dendritic stretches with a newly appearing spine were contacted more frequently by microglia in a preceding imaging session than stable spines.
evidence: This is a summary of a primary finding from the study.

claim: Reducing neuronal activity by anesthesia reduced microglia-spine interaction, but did not affect the relationship between contact and turnover.
source: Reducing neuronal activity by anesthesia reduced microglia-spine interaction, but did not affect the aforementioned relationship between contact and turnover.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the study.

claim: Clustered events of spine gain or loss were associated with higher microglial contact frequency.
source: Furthermore, clustered events of spine gain or loss were associated with higher microglial contact frequency.
evidence: This is a summary of a finding from the study.

claim: Recent findings indicate that there is considerable effect on microglia by the volatile narcotic isoflurane via THIK-1 channels, which reduces microglial scanning activity in vitro in the hippocampus.
source: Recent findings indicate that there is considerable effect on microglia by the volatile narcotic isoflurane via THIK-1 channels, which reduces microglial scanning activity in vitro in the hippocampus (Madry et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Madry et al., 2018.

claim: Reduced microglial fine process motility was observed in anesthetized mice compared to awake conditions in the hippocampus in vivo.
source: Here, we investigate microglial motility in the hippocampus in vivo, where we observed reduced microglial fine process motility in anesthetized mice compared to awake conditions.

claim: The decreased microglial motility observed in anesthetized mice may be due to reduced neuronal activity.
source: Our data suggest that this decreased microglial motility may be due to reduced neuronal activity.

claim: Applying TTX to the hippocampus reduced microglial motility in awake mice.
source: Applying TTX to the hippocampus reduced microglial motility in awake mice.

claim: In previous experiments, neuronal activity might have already been reduced by the use of anesthetics or been altered in the preparation of slice cultures.

claim: Region-specific microglia mRNA expression profiles could contribute to the motility difference between cortex and hippocampus.
source: Region-specific microglia mRNA expression profiles could contribute to the motility difference between cortex and hippocampus (Grabert et al., 2016).

claim: TTX is a potent blocker of voltage-gated sodium channels and may directly affect microglia, as they express TTX-sensitive sodium channels.
source: Furthermore, TTX is a potent blocker of voltage-gated sodium channels and may directly affect microglia, as they express TTX-sensitive sodium channels.

source: TTX application in vitro reduces microglial phagocytosis and lamellipodia formation (Black et al., 2009; Persson et al., 2014).

claim: Silencing CA3 neurons (and their input to CA1 via Schaffer collaterals) reduced microglial motility in the SR of the CA1.
source: In our study, silencing CA3 neurons (and their input to CA1 via Schaffer collaterals) reduced microglial motility in the SR of the CA1.

claim: Isoflurane anesthesia increased microglial arborization and motility in the cortex in vivo.

claim: Other studies identified increased arborization alone (area coverage by microglia) in the cortex under isoflurane anesthesia.
source: In contrast to our observations in the hippocampus, isoflurane anesthesia increased microglial arborization and motility in the cortex in vivo (Liu et al., 2019), while other studies identified increased arborization alone (area coverage by microglia) (Sun et al., 2019; Umpierre et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Stowell et al. showed effects on microglial arborization under a mixture of fentanyl, midazolam, and dexmedetomidine arguing for a noradrenergic regulation of microglial surveillance.
source: Stowell et al. showed effects on microglial arborization under a mixture of fentanyl, midazolam, and dexmedetomidine arguing for a noradrenergic regulation of microglial surveillance (Stowell et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Stowell et al., 2019.

claim: Both ketamine/xylazine or pentobarbital administration decreased microglial motility.
source: Other non-isoflurane anesthetics had the opposite effect on microglial motility; both ketamine/xylazine or pentobarbital administration decreased microglial motility (Hristovska et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hristovska et al., 2020.

claim: The data clearly indicate that neuronal activity and neurotransmitter release regulate microglial motility.
